facts.statement: The study used brain recordings from people and their real-time judgments of a soundtrack containing speech and music to test if basic sound features are enough to tell the two apart.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The brain's sound-processing areas followed the timing and pitch changes of the audio, using different types of brain waves to handle the timing versus the pitch.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The brain activity patterns for these sound features were able to predict how a separate group of people categorized the sounds as speech or music.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The left side of the brain was better at tracking the features of speech, while the right side was better at tracking the features of music.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results suggest that the brain's basic coding of sound features is enough to distinguish speech from music, without needing more complex abstract processing.
facts.subject: humans
